stem: An order service in account B must invoke a Lambda function and send messages to an SQS queue, both owned by account A, without assuming a role in account A. The service's role in account B already allows lambda:InvokeFunction and sqs:SendMessage on those ARNs. Which TWO changes in account A complete the setup? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Attach an SCP in account A's organization that allows account B to invoke the function and send messages
Add a statement to the function's resource-based policy that allows account B to call lambda:InvokeFunction
Add a queue policy that allows the account B role to perform sqs:SendMessage on the queue
Attach a permissions boundary to the function's execution role that lists account B as a trusted caller
Create a role in account A that trusts account B's role, and have the account B role call sts:AssumeRole on it before invoking the function and sending the messages

rationale: Lambda functions and SQS queues both support resource-based policies. A statement in the function policy (added with add-permission or put-resource-policy) lets account B invoke the function, and a queue policy that names the account B role allows sqs:SendMessage. Together with the role's identity-based policy, both halves of cross-account access are in place. An SCP never grants permissions. A permissions boundary on the execution role only limits what the function itself can do; it does not control who may invoke it. A role in account A that trusts account B and is reached by calling sts:AssumeRole is a common cross-account pattern, but the stem rules it out here: the order service must invoke the function and send the messages without assuming a role in account A, and its own identity-based policy already allows both actions directly once the resource-based policies above are in place.
